reason: The quotation is not a sentence, and its full stop is minted. I fetched the very page the evidence cites (history.hanover.edu/courses/excerpts/165pisan.html) and read the opening verbatim: “One day as I was sitting alone in my study surrounded by books on all kinds of subjects, devoting myself to literary studies, my usual habit, my mind dwelt at length on the weighty opinions of various authors whom I had studied for a long time.” The verifier cuts after “subjects” and replaces the edition’s comma with a full stop at a point where the syntax has not resolved: “One day as I was sitting alone in my study surrounded by books on all kinds of subjects.” is a subordinate clause with no main clause, so the card would print an unfinished sentence. The month’s own precedent for a cut, 03-poet-01, stops at a complete clause (“For use almost can change the stamp of nature”); this stops mid-construction. The source line then compounds the fault by naming the locator as “the opening sentence” while printing about a third of it, so the locator as printed on the card is false. Two further weaknesses. First, the translation is asserted, not evidenced: the Hanover page credits no translator at all (it names only two unattributed course texts supplied by Anne Kelsch and S. Spishak), and the note concedes the Persea printing was never opened, so nothing in the evidence ties this wording to Richards except the verifier’s say-so. The wording is consistent with Richards 1982 and is plainly not Brown-Grant’s 1999 Penguin, but a track whose stated failure mode is translation drift should not name a translator on an uncredited web excerpt. Second, on rule 3 this fails the month: scene-setting about sitting among books is neither wisdom nor counsel, and May is Wisdom and Counsel. Not shipped, not near-shipped, not banned, Christine de Pizan at 0 of 3 (shipped.js run), so the person and the scope of the work are fine; the defect is editorial and it is fixable by restoring the sentence.
